title: Why Modelling Matters as Much as Didau Says, With Less Nuance
author: Salles, Dominic
summary: In direct response to David Didau's five principles of effective modelling, Dominic Salles argues that nuance—however expert—is the enemy of teacher progress because it introduces complexity teachers cannot hold under cognitive load and will default away from. His counter-framework collapses into one mantra: 1 visualiser, 2 models (good and excellent), 3 criteria. He works through each of Didau's five principles and shows how the simple routine addresses each without requiring the expert distinctions Didau draws. On comparison, the routine delivers it automatically through paired models. On structure, teaching an explicit essay or paragraph structure alongside the model transfers it to new questions. On attention, the 3 criteria do the work. On non-examples, the visualiser surfaces them from student work in real time. On live modelling, the visualiser outperforms explanation because student work output is the feedback. His key reframe: even imperfect modelling with a simple system will improve outcomes more reliably than nuanced modelling that never gets deployed—a bad teacher will be much less bad, a good teacher will be great. Step 7 is added at the close: students never copy; everything is from memory.
points: Nuance—however expert—is the enemy of teacher progress because it introduces the kind of uncertainty that causes teachers to fall back on habit; simplicity wins not because it's optimal but because it gets deployed.

The core routine—1 visualiser, 2 models (good and excellent), 3 criteria—passes the cognitive load test, the split-attention test, the teacher-talk test, and the 'I wasn't listening—what do I have to do?' test simultaneously.

The visualiser replaces many of the expert-level decisions in Didau's principles: non-examples surface from real student work in real time, comparisons happen automatically against the models, and feedback loops close within the lesson.

Even when a model covers the same content as the student task (Didau's worst case), students still gain deep subject knowledge, embedded structural understanding, and disciplinary literacy from the exercise of reproducing it from memory.

A bad teacher using the routine will be much less bad; a good teacher using it will be great—the floor rises without requiring anyone to develop the expert judgment that nuanced frameworks assume is already present.
quotes: Nuance is the enemy of progress. Nuance is a host of exceptions, of buts, of if this, then that, but if that, then something else - it is complex. Complexity is uncertainty, and uncertainty is death to progress.
Nuance is not wrong. It is simply not useful - it is a barrier.
If you always focus on just 3 criteria, your students will understand better how to write in your subject (even if I, as a self appointed expert, would pick different, more nuanced criteria).

3 criteria will always pass the cognitive load test, the split attention problem, the teacher talk problem, the flexibility of teacher time problem, the I-wasn’t-really-listening-what-do-I-have-to-do problem. It is short and clear, and students can do something with it really quickly.
A bad teacher will be much less bad. A good teacher will be great.
Simply modelling teaches much more than your 3 criteria. Each model meets the student where they are.
So, once again, just having a system for picking books/work at random to put under the visualiser will do the job for you. 1 visualiser, 2 models, 3 criteria will always work.
Students never copy. There are no exceptions. Everything is from memory.
